newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac-Jospin meet about Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac-Jospin meet about Amsterdam summit.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin met on Saturday to define France's position ahead of a European Union summit in Amsterdam amidst continuing disagreement with Germany on how to proceed towards a single currency.
Jospin arrived at the Elysee palace accompanied by Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn and European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici.

There was no indication how long the talks would last but officials said reporters would not be allowed into the palace and it was not immediately clear whether a statement would be issued afterwards.
The meeting was called after a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, failed on Friday to resolve differences on a single currency.
The French leaders were to discuss further steps, with Europe now facing an uphill task to strike a deal on an EU stability pact in time for the summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.
Strauss-Kahn told reporters earlier in the day that reaching agreement with Germany at the EU summit would be hard but progress was being made.
"The Germans have understood they must make a step forward if they want things to advance and we have to do the same," he said.

"Mutual concessions are the very definition of co-operation between two countries. I have the impression things are moving -- it's difficult, but things are moving and I hope we will reach agreement in Amsterdam," Strauss-Kahn said.
Jospin said in Poitiers the new government was committed to a single currency but wanted a fundamentally new approach to monetary union.
Demands for a focus on growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of a single currency, he said.
Aides quoted Jospin as having told the Socialist meeting in Paris, mostly devoted to domestic issues, that he would not accept a simple "social addendum" to the stability treaty.

Jospin told the meeting he believed he was speaking for other European peoples and not only for his own, when he said growth, development, employment and the fight against inequality should have equal footing as a priority with monetary stability in the pact.

Socialist first secretary Francois Hollande told reporters Jospin wanted the EU to revive a project it had approved, but never acted upon, to create hundreds of thousands of jobs across western Europe by launching major public works projects, especially connected with transport.
The plan, adoped at a summit in Essen, Germany, in 1994 included new EU-financed highways and high-speed railway lines.
France's new government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1, raised its objections to the pact for the first time on Monday.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, whose country does not intend to introduce single currency soon said that Britain would back "certain changes so that community institutions take their decisions in better conditions.
"We are going to have to imagine other ways to give employment to all, to make the single market work better because this will permit jobs to be created," he told the weekly Le Journal du Dimanche.
He said Britain would back the EU's social chapter, wanted a reform of agricultural policies "and above all, put employment at the top of our priorities".
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in Poitiers there would be intensive talks among European officials at the weekend to try to strike a deal.
Both France and Germany are keen to avoid any suggestion of a rift between Paris and Bonn, whose alliance is seen as crucial to pushing monetary union through in 1999.
